title: Lower Extremity Swelling Differential Diagnosis
description: Differential diagnosis for unilateral and bilateral lower extremity swelling in adults, covering venous, lymphatic, infectious, cardiac, and systemic etiologies with emphasis on distinguishing acute from chronic and unilateral from bilateral presentations.
source_description: Ely JW, Osheroff JA, Chambliss ML, Ebell MH. Approach to Leg Edema of Unclear Etiology. J Am Board Fam Med 2006;19(2):148-160.

diagnoses.name: Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT)
key_features: Acute unilateral leg swelling (onset within 72 hours)
Pitting edema with tenderness
Calf or thigh pain, worse with dorsiflexion
Increased warmth over affected area
Erythema along the course of the deep veins
red_flags: Massive swelling with phlegmasia cerulea dolens (limb-threatening)
Concurrent pleuritic chest pain or dyspnea suggesting PE

diagnoses.name: Cellulitis
key_features: Unilateral erythema with spreading warmth
Fever and systemic symptoms
Tenderness and induration of affected area
Often follows skin break, wound, or tinea pedis
red_flags: Pain out of proportion to exam findings
recommended_tests: Blood cultures if systemic signs present
Duplex ultrasonography to exclude concurrent DVT

diagnoses.name: Chronic Venous Insufficiency
key_features: Bilateral or unilateral dependent edema, worse at end of day
Improves with elevation overnight
Brawny reddish-hued skin predilection for medial ankle
Hemosiderin deposition and stasis dermatitis
Venous ulcerations over medial malleolus in advanced disease

diagnoses.name: Heart Failure
key_features: Bilateral symmetric pitting edema
Jugular venous distention
Dyspnea on exertion and orthopnea
Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea
Weight gain from fluid retention

diagnoses.name: Lymphedema
key_features: Chronic progressive non-pitting edema (late stage)
Pitting in early stages before fibrosis develops
Dorsal foot and toe swelling (squared-off digits)
Positive Kaposi-Stemmer sign (inability to tent skin of dorsal second toe)
Brawny, thickened, verrucous skin in advanced disease
red_flags: Rapid unilateral onset suggesting malignant lymphatic obstruction
New lymphedema with pelvic or inguinal mass
recommended_tests: CT or MRI if malignant obstruction suspected

diagnoses.name: Medication-Induced Edema
key_features: Bilateral soft pitting edema
Onset weeks after initiating offending medication
Resolves within days of discontinuation
Common culprits: calcium channel blockers, NSAIDs, corticosteroids, thiazolidinediones, estrogen/testosterone

diagnoses.name: Nephrotic Syndrome
key_features: Bilateral pitting edema, often periorbital in morning
Proteinuria (>3.5 g/day) and hypoalbuminemia
Frothy urine
Associated hyperlipidemia
red_flags: Concurrent DVT or renal vein thrombosis (hypercoagulable state)

diagnoses.name: Hepatic Cirrhosis
key_features: Bilateral pitting edema with ascites
Jaundice, spider angiomata, palmar erythema
History of hepatitis or alcohol use disorder
Hypoalbuminemia

diagnoses.name: Pulmonary Hypertension / Cor Pulmonale
key_features: Bilateral lower extremity edema with exertional dyspnea
Often associated with obstructive sleep apnea
Daytime somnolence, loud snoring, neck circumference >17 inches
Elevated jugular venous pressure

diagnoses.name: Idiopathic Edema
key_features: Bilateral edema in premenopausal women
Cyclic pattern related to menstrual cycle
Weight fluctuation >1.4 kg from morning to evening
Diagnosis of exclusion after systemic causes ruled out
recommended_tests: Complete systemic workup to exclude other causes

also_consider.name: Compartment Syndrome
also_consider.rationale: Acute limb-threatening condition after trauma or reperfusion; pain out of proportion to exam with tense swelling requires emergent surgical evaluation

also_consider.name: Ruptured Baker Cyst
also_consider.rationale: Posterior knee cyst rupture mimics DVT with acute calf swelling and pain; confirm with knee and calf ultrasound

also_consider.name: May-Thurner Syndrome (Iliac Vein Compression)
also_consider.rationale: Left iliac vein compressed by right iliac artery causing left-sided DVT or chronic swelling; consider in young women with left leg predominance

also_consider.name: Lipedema
also_consider.rationale: Symmetric adipose deposition in legs sparing feet; almost exclusively in women; does not improve with elevation or weight loss

also_consider.name: Hypothyroidism (Myxedema)
also_consider.rationale: Generalized non-pitting edema with periorbital swelling and skin thickening; check TSH in bilateral edema of unclear cause

also_consider.name: Complex Regional Pain Syndrome
also_consider.rationale: Unilateral edema with pain, allodynia, and vasomotor changes weeks after trauma; diagnosis based on Budapest criteria

also_consider.name: Pretibial Myxedema (Graves Disease)
also_consider.rationale: Localized non-pitting edema of pretibial area in Graves disease; distinct orange-peel texture

also_consider.name: Musculoskeletal Injury (Fracture, Muscle Tear)
also_consider.rationale: Acute unilateral swelling after trauma; most common cause of acute unilateral leg swelling in emergency settings (up to 40%)

also_consider.name: Pelvic Mass or Tumor Compressing Iliac Veins
also_consider.rationale: Unilateral or bilateral leg edema from extrinsic venous or lymphatic compression; consider CT pelvis in unexplained proximal edema

also_consider.name: Constrictive Pericarditis
also_consider.rationale: Bilateral edema with elevated JVP and Kussmaul sign; consider when heart failure treatment is ineffective

also_consider.name: Inferior Vena Cava Obstruction
also_consider.rationale: Bilateral leg edema with prominent abdominal collateral veins; may be caused by thrombosis, tumor, or filter complications

also_consider.name: Filariasis (Lymphatic)
also_consider.rationale: Endemic parasitic cause of lymphedema in tropical regions; consider in patients from endemic areas with chronic leg swelling

clinical_reasoning_prompt: This is an evidence-based reference set, not an exhaustive differential. Distinguish unilateral from bilateral swelling as the first branch point: acute unilateral swelling requires urgent DVT evaluation, while chronic bilateral edema more often reflects systemic disease. Always assess for medication causes, consider the tempo of onset (acute vs chronic), and examine for pitting vs non-pitting character. In patients with unilateral swelling and negative DVT workup, consider Baker cyst, musculoskeletal injury, and lymphatic obstruction. In bilateral edema, evaluate cardiac, hepatic, and renal function before attributing to venous insufficiency.
